canberra.title: Meep, meep! Wile E. Coyote dodged Warner’s anvil to deliver box-office dynamite
canberra.snippet: The Looney Tunes have been a staple of pop culture for decades, with the likes of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig being among the mo...
canberra.content:
Looney Tunes have returned to the big screen with a movie that almost never came out: Coyote vs. ACME. Photo: Ketchup Entertainment.

The Looney Tunes have been a staple of pop culture for decades, with the likes of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig being among the most recognisable characters in entertainment.

However, despite being animated icons of the 20th century, the wacky band of misfit cartoon animals have struggled to stay in the limelight in recent years, with several movies bombing at the box office and even bankable TV shows failing to stay on air.

Despite the poor run of form in the last two decades, the Looney Tunes are back in 2026 with Coyote vs. ACME, the movie that almost never came out, despite finishing production in 2023.

Original producers Warner Bros. set out to dispose of the movie as a tax write-off, believing it wouldn’t recoup the $70 million it spent to make.

Thankfully, despite all the corporate drama behind the film, production company Ketchup Entertainment brought the movie back from the dead, striking a deal to buy the rights for $50 million.

Now amassing $100 million at the global box office, Coyote vs. ACME has proven to be well worth the bailout by being one of the funniest movies of the year.

The story here is simple enough. Wile E. Coyote is fed up with being blown up, squashed, crashed and bashed by all the items he’s used to try to catch the Road Runner.

To make up for all his pain, Coyote decides to take the manufacturer, ACME, to court for damages with the help of reluctant injury lawyer Kevin Avery (Will Forte).

Coyote vs. ACME is a joke-a-second, 100-minute gem that deserves to be seen on the big screen. This film has so much heart, and it’s clear the writers, including James Gunn, care deeply about these characters.

They take a bit that spawned countless three-minute cartoons and bring it all together into a film that might be the best live-action/animated hybrid since Who Framed Roger Rabbit.

The animation is also a selling point (as you’d expect). It’s not the super glossy computer-generated look seen in other hybrid films, but it’s also not all hand-drawn. It makes for characters that feel like cartoons in the real world, without diving into the uncanny valley.

Nailing this look mattered, since the Coyote and Road Runner famously don’t talk. Instead, we are shown their perspective through the way they are animated, and it’s done to perfection.

The other side of the coin is the performances from the live-action actors, acting opposite the animations. The best example here is Will Forte as Kevin and John Cena as ACME’s lawyer, Buddy Crane.

Both these guys understood exactly what movie they were in. They’re not trying to win awards or create content for sizzle reels. They deliver the comedy and pacing you’d expect from a movie featuring the Looney Tunes.

That said, when the movie dives into more mature themes, Forte delivers.

The courtroom drama here is also very enjoyable. Don’t expect the likes of A Few Good Men or even Suits, but the setting drives much of what happens here, and it delivers some of the best lines in the film.

While all the new stuff is great, an understated part of the film is how it honours the near 100-year history of its source material.

Scattered throughout, clips from the famous cartoons dating back to the 1930s appear, mainly to reinforce, in Coyote’s case, the years of harm he’s endured.

Whether intentional or not, it creates a real sense of familiarity with these characters, driving home that, at least subconsciously, everyone has spent time watching the Looney Tunes at some point or another.

Coyote vs. ACME is a blast (excuse the pun). It’s a perfect film for families who want a laugh with a hint of maturity behind it. The story of the movie’s development is worth telling alone, but with its box-office success, you’ve got to ask why this movie was almost buried forever – and what other gems are studios sitting on?

Coyote vs. ACME is now showing in cinemas across the country (that’s all, folks).

canberra.title: Tender confirms Access Canberra shopfront move to Woden Library, upstairs
canberra.snippet: Plans to relocate the Access Canberra Woden Shopfront to Woden Library show how much has changed since the heady days of reimagining what...
canberra.content:
The Access Canberra shopfront will move to level 1 of the Woden Library. Photo: Region.

Plans to relocate the Access Canberra Woden Shopfront to Woden Library show how much has changed since the heady days of reimagining what a library could be for the community.

A tender has been released for the design and construction of the new shopfront – not back in its old location next to the library but upstairs on level 1, where a $2.243 million 2021 makeover created a new world of relaxation, work and art spaces, and innovative recording studios for music and podcasts.

Occupied by the ACT Heritage Library for many years before it moved to Fyshwick, the floor was reimagined as a multi-use facility where users can read, study or work, take a dance or yoga lesson, brainstorm a business idea, or put down tracks and record a podcast.

Libraries ACT Executive Branch Manager Vanessa Little said at the time people had been asking to access the building after hours for some time, and libraries were very much evolving into these sorts of community spaces.

“So yes, this is very much 21st-century library progression and whilst books are still really important … we are mixing that around now with all of these other activities,” she said.

Five years later, it’s back to the future with a twist. Access Canberra will now occupy that multi-use space.

City and Government Services Minister Tara Cheyne had flagged the return of the shopfront to the library building.

The move comes as library hours are wound back to contain costs and, Ms Cheyne said, as a bid to fix underlying staffing and culture issues following last year’s scathing review of library services.

The Legislative Assembly censured her for her efforts, and the Woden relocation will also have its critics.

In July, independent MLA Fiona Carrick called on the ACT Government to release the business case behind the move, questioning whether the proposal is being driven by community outcomes or by a lease expiry and cost-saving objectives.

She said the community feared it would mean losing further amenity in the Woden Town Centre.

Infrastructure Canberra says the project will bring Access Canberra Woden Service Centre and Woden Library together in a “co-located community hub in the heart of the Woden Town Centre, ensuring residents continue to have access to both services close to home”.

“The project will reconfigure and enhance the existing government-owned building to support both services, with improvements such as enhanced wayfinding and updates to customer facilities,” it says.

The refurbished Woden Library, 2021 retro style. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

What will happen to the upstairs spaces? That’s not quite clear.

Infrastructure Canberra says some study spaces on level 1 will likely be relocated to the ground floor.

Existing community rooms on both levels will remain available for community use, with minor changes being considered to make better use of the available space.

The new Service Centre will still retain 12 counters and remain an “inclusive and supportive space for Canberrans to undertake government services and transactions”.

Infrastructure Canberra says it is working closely with Libraries ACT to maintain a welcoming, accessible and functional experience for users.

Be assured the result will be better for all.

“The project will help create a better integrated community facility, supporting access to library services, government services and community meeting spaces in a single location,” Infrastructure Canberra says.

The tender opened on Friday, 25 September, and will close on 29 October 2026. But we can’t tell you much more because the tender documents are confidential.

But a head contractor will be appointed to work with the ACT Government on the detailed design before refurbishment works begin.

Community and stakeholder engagement will occur over the coming months, which will inform the detailed design, with a particular focus on accessibility.

Meetings, stakeholder workshops and information displays will be held at both the Woden Library and the current Access Canberra Woden Shopfront.

To stay updated, Infrastructure Canberra says people can subscribe for further information.

canberra.title: The Supermum life hack nobody wanted, but actually works (and that’s really irritating)
canberra.snippet: This week, Georgie Dent, CEO of independent parent advocacy organisation The Parenthood, made a glaringly obvious point at the National P...
canberra.content:
If you’ve ever looked longingly upon a cool, calm and collected working Mum and thought, “How does she do it?” – Well, have I got news for you? Photo: Hayley Nicholls

This week, Georgie Dent, CEO of independent parent advocacy organisation The Parenthood, made a glaringly obvious point at the National Press Club: Aussie parents need more time.

814 hours of care a year, to be exact.

That’s how much extra care two full-time-working parents with primary-school-aged children need to find.

Ms Dent spoke about the mismatch between standard work and school hours, and the way our modern society operates around an outdated model in which every household had a “spare adult” at home.

And that doesn’t touch the admin hours required to keep a home – and career – on track.

Of course, these days there’s rarely a “homemaker” behind the scenes. And it’s largely fallen on women to develop a double life, because in most families, women remain the primary carers and carriers of the domestic load – and that barely leaves room for the most flexible full-time job.

That’s why – around the school gate – I’m fascinated when I identify those superhuman women who are managing to be Mum while also carrying particularly demanding careers.

Accomplished lawyers, defence procurement specialists, high-ranking government officials whose job you’re not allowed to know.

One of these Mums literally commands a ship.

It’s difficult to conceive of a job less compatible with managing a primary school schedule – whether at sea or posted ashore – but this woman is doing it like a boss. Often, in high heels and aviators. She is a literal hero.

In fact, she is usually the one reminding me about play dates and permission slips.

Another Wonder Woman somehow manages to spend the day as a high-powered lawyer and still show up at pick-up with a Tupperware container full of snacks.

So the obvious question is, “How do they do it?”

Well, I started asking them – because my superpower is being nosy.

And what I found was equal parts exhilarating and infuriating.

They’re getting up in the middle of the night.

“It’s very much my go-to for overflow,” one Mum whispered as we waited for assembly to start.

“If I’ve got a time-sensitive project or demanding client, I’ll get up at 3:30 and knock out a few hours before everyone wakes up.”

I was agape as my brain tried to imagine such an early hour.

By then, I’ve scarcely finished my revenge bedtime procrastination! Far from whipping the laptop out, I’ve not long found sleep after a late-night deep dive into whatever obscure content category I fell into after the kids finally went unconscious.

Later, at a community fundraising event, another Supermum revealed her source of power.

“Exercise was the thing I couldn’t fit in. That’s why I started getting up at 4 am,” she said, adding, “the trouble is I still stay up late to get that downtime, too.”

By this point, I was incensed. Mums are literally sacrificing sleep – a basic need – to steal time. And we use that time not to pursue our own interests but to care for others, fulfil work commitments or stay healthy.

I was indignant. I was outraged. I was jealous. Wait … what?

With frustration, I realised that this life hack – while it shouldn’t be necessary – was sure to help me too. So, I tried it.

Eyes wide with disbelief, I hesitantly set my alarm for 4 am. I popped my slippers beside the bed.

In the lounge room, I pulled the coffee table to one side and replaced it with a yoga mat. I laid my laptop out suggestively. And went to sleep.

Milliseconds later, the dreaded upbeat synth sounded and – to my utter confusion – my body bounced out of bed.

My feet found warmth, my mouth found coffee, and my body took itself through some light stretches. I watched the news. I checked my emails. Knocked over admin. Honest to God, I even went for a 15-minute jog.

By the time my lazy family appeared – bleary-eyed and barely cognisant – I felt I had lived an entire lifetime. And I’d done it all uninterrupted.

Far from my usual routine of waking to an already hectic household of spilled milk, forbidden Netflix, craft explosions and other sensory assaults, this morning I had a head start on the chaos.

And while my body had jerked out of bed and gone through motions with army-like diligence, my mind had been left to rise slowly in its own time.

I felt bloody great.

True, by evening I was a shell of a human being. But that just meant I was too exhausted to doom-scroll or comfort-watch 90s TV shows.

Basically, I replaced my worst hours with golden hours I did not know existed.

I realise “getting up early” doesn’t sound like a revolutionary life hack – but as far as I’m concerned, anything pre-5 am is the middle of the night.

Of course, women shouldn’t need to sacrifice sleep to make ends meet. But here we are.

We didn’t make the bed, and we don’t have time to lie in it.

canberra.title: Yes, Virginia, there really is a platypus hiding in Lake Burley Griffin
canberra.snippet: A very special visitor has made a home in Lake Burley Griffin, but experts say its rare presence isn’t unusual. Canberra content cr...
canberra.content:
27 September 2026

Start the conversation

There isn’t much for the platypus to eat in Lake Burley Griffin, says Waterwatch’s Daniel Harris-Pascal. Photo: ACT Government.

A very special visitor has made a home in Lake Burley Griffin, but experts say its rare presence isn’t unusual.

Canberra content creator Daniel Morton Jones (also known as themortz) shared the video on Instagram this week.

In the post, he said the video had been sent to him and showed a platypus taking a dip in Lake Burley Griffin.

“It’s amazing some of the things you can spot in our little city,” he wrote in the caption.

“All you have to do is stop and take a moment to have a look and sure enough you’ll spot some pretty amazing local wildlife.”

So why did this particular platypus find its way into the lake and how?

Upper Murrumbidgee Waterwatch citizen science facilitator Daniel Harris-Pascal says it’s not the first time one has taken a holiday there.

“We’ve definitely seen it before,” he tells Region.

Waterwatch data reveals that, just in the last five years, at least 20 people have seen platypuses in Lake Burley Griffin.

This year’s Platypus Month surveys found 37 platypuses making their homes across the region.

Mr Harris-Pascal reckons that one male platypus might have “turfed” another one out of a territory.

After all, this time of year is when the platypus breed, meaning competition could have been fierce.

“They can end up in less ideal places to live,” he said of that scenario.

“We will sometimes find them in local wetlands or people’s backyard pools, stormwater drains – places that they won’t persist, but that they’re just trying to have a crack at getting established and finding enough to eat.”

He says that while it’s not a common sight, he’s not expecting the platypus to stay there for too long, pointing to the cement edge of the lake.

“Platypuses don’t tend to live long-term [periods] in Lake Burley Griffin and partly that’s because there probably aren’t enough good-quality water bugs to sustain them.

“But also, it’s not a site that’s got very good spots for platypus habitat, in terms of things like natural riverbanks and good vegetation.”

For Mr Harris-Pascal, the sighting shows the importance of keeping our waterways clean.

“I think people have this vision that platypuses are going to only be living in the pristine waters of Namadgi or Tidbinbilla.

“The reality is that platypuses are a very urban creature. They can persist in urban waterways if they’re good quality enough.”

He encourages people to keep stormwater as clean as possible, such as by picking up their dog’s waste and “O-shaped litter” (things like milk bottles and rubber bands that a platypus can get caught in).

“When it rains, that stormwater picks up all the pollutants and takes them down into the creeks untreated, which impacts our platypus,” he says.

The need to keep the environment clean is echoed by WIRES.

A spokesperson told Region that heavy rainfall could wash a platypus away from their normal territory.

“[It] is feasible that platypuses could access the lake in search of food if the species has already been identified as being present in any of these waterways,” the spokesperson said.

If you find a platypus and are concerned you can let WIRES know by calling 1300 904 737 or by completing an online form.
