canberra.title: Telescopes, 3D printers and late-night access: Is this Canberra’s library of the future?
canberra.snippet: Canberra’s libraries have become an unlikely political battleground, with reduced opening hours sparking petitions, Assembly motion...
canberra.content:
What do you want from your local library — books, longer opening hours, new technology or more community spaces? Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Canberra’s libraries have become an unlikely political battleground, with reduced opening hours sparking petitions, Assembly motions and, last week, the censure of a government minister.

Now the debate is moving beyond when libraries should open to what they should actually offer.

Could Canberrans borrow a telescope instead of buying one? Use a 3D printer or podcast studio at their local branch? Borrow tools and household equipment? Or enter a library after hours when no staff are there?

ACT Greens municipal services spokesperson Andrew Braddock is asking Canberrans to put forward ideas for the future of the city’s libraries, including after-hours self-access, smaller neighbourhood library points, spaces for making and repairing things, and becoming a ‘Library of Things’.

“Imagine finishing work late and still having somewhere safe and free to study. Borrowing a telescope with your kids. Using a 3D printer. Recording a podcast. Borrowing something you only need once instead of buying it,” Mr Braddock said.

“That might sound like the library of the future. In plenty of places, it is already the library of today.”

The ideas are already being tried elsewhere.

Melbourne libraries offer makerspaces with 3D printers, laser cutters, embroidery machines and podcast recording equipment, while Adelaide’s library network provides equipment including 3D printers, digital drawing tablets, photo scanners and green screens.

Monash Public Library Service has a Library of Things, where members can borrow practical items such as induction cooktops, cake tins and hand tools.

Mr Braddock believes Canberra should consider similar models.

“ACT libraries could include better after-hours access, smaller neighbourhood library points, spaces to make and repair things, and Libraries of Things where people can borrow useful equipment instead of having to buy it,” he said.

The push comes after months of debate about the state of Canberra’s library network.

More than 3500 people signed Mr Braddock’s petition calling for investment in libraries, while the Legislative Assembly passed a motion calling on the government to pause the removal of Sunday opening.

That fight escalated last week when City and Government Services Minister Tara Cheyne was censured 13 votes to 10 over the government’s decision to proceed with reduced library hours. Opposition Leader Mark Parton accused the minister of having “ignored” the earlier Assembly motion. Ms Cheyne defended her handling of the issue, citing the operational pressures facing the library network.

Those pressures extend well beyond opening hours.

An independent review of Libraries ACT found problems with staffing, rostering and workplace culture, including mistrust between frontline staff and management. It was commissioned after concerns about repeated unplanned closures, poor staff morale and whether the existing service was sustainable.

But the debate over the future of libraries is also increasingly about what role they should play in their communities.

A national Libraries as Social Cohesion Hubs initiative gives some indication of how far that role can extend.

Across nine months, 115 public library services and 10 university libraries delivered 744 programs aimed at strengthening community connections and reducing isolation.

The programs reached families, seniors, First Nations people, culturally and linguistically diverse communities, people with disability and young people, with more than 180,000 engagements recorded.

That shifts the conversation away from libraries simply being places to borrow books.

They can be free places to study or work, learn a skill, meet other people, access technology or use equipment that may otherwise be unaffordable.

And that is the conversation Mr Braddock now wants Canberra to have.

“If we want libraries that remain relevant for the next generation, we need to think beyond books and opening hours and build services around how people actually live, learn, and connect,” he said.

After months of political argument over closing library doors, Canberrans are now being asked what they would like to see behind them.

Readers can send their ideas to Mr Braddock at Braddock@parliament.act.gov.au or join the conversation on Canberra Greens Facebook and Instagram pages.

australia.title: Melbourne man’s mysterious disappearance on popular Peru hiking trail prompts widespread search
australia.snippet: Loved ones describe Jordan Yap, 30, as an experienced hiker who set out for a 10-day solo trek Peru before falling silent Get our breakin...
australia.content:
Loved ones of a missing Australian trekker who was last seen nearly two weeks ago on a remote South American hiking trail are urging local authorities to help with the search.

A wide-scale sweep by a private rescue crew has so far failed to find any trace of 30-year-old Jordan Yap, who last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru’s Huayhuash mountain range, 400km north-east of Lima.

He was last seen near the beginning of his trek across the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, which is regarded as a challenging, high-altitude trek through the remote Andes mountains.

Regarded as a very experienced hiker by friends and family, the Melbourne man failed to make contact on Wednesday, his estimated return date.

He also failed to check back into the Krusty Hostel in Huaraz, where his luggage remains stored, and missed a scheduled flight from Lima to Cusco on Thursday.

“It’s really uncharacteristic of him to not have communicated at any point in his journey if he had the chance to,” longtime friend Kevin Nguyen said.

“It is a very popular trek, where you might have 200 to 300 hikers and guides per week during the busy season, so it is very uncharacteristic that no one’s seen him since day one or day two.”

The avid trekker misplaced a satellite beacon he was travelling with days before he set off on the 120km hike, raising further concerns.

Local mountain rescue organisation Socorro Andino Peruano has been hired by Yap’s family to help with the search.

His loved ones are holding out hope the rescue group, which recently rescued a Canadian trekker from the same trail, will be able to find him safe.

“Time is of the essence … because ultimately, as much as we were saying he’s been missing since the 23rd, he’s had no contact with anyone since the 14th,” Nguyen said.

Rescue crews completed their biggest day of search operations so far on Saturday (Sunday morning AEST), scouring various trails on the circuit to no avail.

“I know Jordan likes to orienteer and navigate and he’s quite an adventurer himself, so I wouldn’t be surprised if he tried an alternative route,” Nguyen said.

Yap had been planning the trek for more than a year and had recently bought a GPS watch to allow for offline maps to guide him on the hike.

“He was telling everyone about how he was ready to go on a big hike like this, (he was) really excited,” Nguyen said.

He was last known to be wearing a white jacket, green sunshade sweater and grey pants.

The experienced trekker was believed to be carrying a 40-litre hiking bag, Durston dome tent and hiking poles.

Family and friends are urging the Australian government to work with Peruvian officials and local authorities to mobilise further resources in and around the rugged region.

The Australian embassy in Peru is helping his family.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has been contacted for comment.

australia.title: AFL grand final breaks TV audience records – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed. Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Deaths in Queensland child protection system reach ...
australia.content:
AFL grand final smashes TV viewership records

The AFL grand final smashed viewership records for Seven yesterday, with the broadcaster saying it was the most watched one ever.

Seven reported a total national TV audience of more than 4.5 million, with an audience reach of 6.5 million. Those figures make it the #1 program on Australian television this year, Seven said.

The pre-game event featuring Kylie Minogue reached more than 4.3 million people, up 20% on the year prior. Chris Jones, Southern Cross Media’s director of sport, said:

From the opening moments of our coverage outside the MCG, through Kylie Minogue’s show-stopping pre-game performance, an unforgettable match and the premiership celebrations, Australians were with us every step of the way.

Earlier today the triple premiership-winning Brisbane team celebrated with fans at the Lions’ spiritual home at Brunswick St Oval in Fitzroy North.

Key events

  • 8h ago

    What we learned, Sunday 27 September

  • 8h ago

    AFL grand final smashes TV viewership records

  • 9h ago

    Marles defends planned sale of defence properties: ‘not a heritage organisation’

  • 11h ago

    New South Wales’ ‘eyes in the sky’ spot a dozen sharks every day

  • 12h ago

    ‘Finger-wagging’ over OpenAI hack not helpful: Jane Hume

  • 12h ago

    Partner of NSW police officer who died says he’s lost the love of his life

  • 13h ago

    Marles says OpenAI CEO didn't tell him about hack in September meeting

  • 13h ago

    Flight cancellations cause heartache for interstate footy fans

  • 13h ago

    Albanese says announcement of Medicare breach ‘purely in national interest’

What we learned, Sunday 27 September

Thanks for sticking with the blog today, here are some highlights:

Richard Marles, the deputy prime minister, said the CEO of OpenAI didn’t tell him about the hack of Australian government websites when they met earlier this month.

Jane Hume, the deputy Liberal leader, said she’s unsure “who they’re going to put in cuffs” after the AI breach.

The partner of Mia Lay, the NSW police officer who died in a car crash while on duty, said she was the “happiest girl I’ve met”, calling her the love of his life.

NSW said drone patrols picked up an average of 20 sharks a day at patrolled beaches over winter as aerial surveillance was being ramped up for the school holidays.

The AFL grand final smashed viewership records, with millions tuning in to watch Kylie Minogue’s pre game performance.

Have a lovely Sunday afternoon, see you tomorrow.

Newcastle fans stymied by train delays, but services running again

Transport NSW advised those travelling from Newcastle to Sydney’s Olympic Park for this afternoon’s NRL match to allow plenty of extra time due to a failed freight train at Warnervale.

Trains have resumed their journeys between Newcastle and Wyong at slower speeds, with some buses helping supplement travel.

Sydney Train’s head of rail operations, Jas Tumber, said earlier:

Diversions are currently in place that will allow train services to move around the failed freight train, however, this is adding at least one hour to journeys.

We apologise for this inconvenience and thank passengers for their patience. Pacific National have mobilised their repair crews to temporarily repair the failed freight train as soon as possible.

AFL grand final smashes TV viewership records

The AFL grand final smashed viewership records for Seven yesterday, with the broadcaster saying it was the most watched one ever.

Seven reported a total national TV audience of more than 4.5 million, with an audience reach of 6.5 million. Those figures make it the #1 program on Australian television this year, Seven said.

The pre-game event featuring Kylie Minogue reached more than 4.3 million people, up 20% on the year prior. Chris Jones, Southern Cross Media’s director of sport, said:

From the opening moments of our coverage outside the MCG, through Kylie Minogue’s show-stopping pre-game performance, an unforgettable match and the premiership celebrations, Australians were with us every step of the way.

Earlier today the triple premiership-winning Brisbane team celebrated with fans at the Lions’ spiritual home at Brunswick St Oval in Fitzroy North.

Joe Hinchliffe

Rookie officer stabbed in Queensland, partner slashed

A police officer has been stabbed in the neck and torso, while his partner reportedly was slashed across the forehead, after responding to a disturbance at a property in Brisbane’s south east.

The police union general president, Shane Prior, told the Courier Mail the rookie officer was “a hero” who held on to his neck to stem the bleeding while trying to chase down and taser his assailant, before having to stop for loss of blood.

The two officers were called to Bogong Street in Hemmant about 5:13am this morning. Police said “officers engaged with two men” before one stabbed the officer and fled on a bike, which he later dumped and continued on foot.

He was arrested about 7am while one officer was transported to hospital and in a stable condition.

OpenAI halts training of latest models as reports mount of AI agents going rogue

OpenAI said it has paused training of its latest artificial intelligence models as reports of AI agents going rogue mount.

The Associated Press reports the decision to halt development came just hours after the company disclosed Friday that it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in which OpenAI agents searching federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information.

Separately, the AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a US Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed.

Read more here:

Marles defends planned sale of defence properties: ‘not a heritage organisation’

The defence minister has fired a warning shot at critics of a plan to sell a historic military barracks, painting the site as a glorified wine cellar that wouldn’t help prevent an attack on Australia.

There are 67 military properties slated to be sold off by the Labor government to raise funds, including Sydney’s Victoria Barracks – a complex established in 1840.

During the week, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, called the site the “spiritual home of the Australian Army” in comments to the Daily Telegraph.

On Sunday, Marles was in no mood to appease his critics.

“It is not my priority for defence to be a heritage organisation,” he told News24.

It’s not my priority to see defence manage the oldest wine cellar in Australia. There are a few former generals who liked hanging out there, who are lamenting this.

The mass sale of defence sites, announced in February, is expected to rake in $1.8bn.

Victoria opposition wants to end prisoner sentence cuts for good behaviour in emergencies

Prisoners shouldn’t have time shaved off their sentences for good behaviour during emergencies, the Victoria opposition argued in its latest election pledge.

AAP reports convicted criminals in Victoria can receive compensatory sentence discounts for good behaviour in unforeseen circumstances, such as industrial disputes and lockdowns, known as emergency management days.

The only laws of their kind in Australia would be abolished if the state’s opposition deposed the Labor government at the November election.

“Labor’s freebie sentence reductions do not meet community expectations and are out of step with other states,” the opposition police and corrections spokesperson, Brad Battin, said on Sunday.

Collectively, nearly 2,300 years were scrubbed from prisoners’ terms over a four years due to the scheme, according to freedom of information documents released to the coalition.

New South Wales’ ‘eyes in the sky’ spot a dozen sharks every day

Drones patrols have picked up an average of 20 sharks a day at patrolled beaches over winter as aerial surveillance is ramped up for the school holidays, AAP reports.

Drone operators across NSW detected 1,225 sharks from 1 July to 31 August, fresh data has revealed.

The shark sightings prompted 360 safety measures, including water evacuations, alarms to alert swimmers and surfers, and the deployment of inflatable boats and jetskis.

Surf Life Saving NSW’s statewide drone operations recorded 49,000 flights, totalling 16,150 hours and covering 343,000 km.

The NSW government released the figures on Sunday as it rolled out “the world’s largest and most advanced aerial shark surveillance program” in time for the state’s school holidays.

Tom McIlroy

‘Competing priorities’ on copyright protections: Hume

Jane Hume has left open the possibility of supporting changes to Australia’s copyright laws to attract more investment by AI companies, ahead of significant legislation expected in the next six months.

On ABC TV, Hume was asked about the differing of views Coalition members on the need to maintain strong protections for Australian writers, musicians, film-makers, photographers and journalists – something the federal government is now considering.

Labor’s AI bill is expected to be debated in parliament early in the new year.

“The copyright laws are really important,” Hume said. “Making sure that we protect the work of authors, artists and journalists, that is fundamentally important.”

Asked about the position of the Liberal frontbencher Michaelia Cash that any move to water down copyright protections would be wrong, Hume was less definitive and cited the role of a new parliamentary committee on AI.

There are competing arguments here. If we want to make sure that any sovereign AI models are culturally relevant and appropriate, we want to make sure that that work is reflected.

There’s a big difference between copying and using illegally other people’s work and learning from it.

We want to work with the government on this to get it right, so that we protect our journalists, protect our authors, protect our artists, but at the same time don’t miss out on the really important access to those frontier AI models that we are going to need, not only to make sure that we are appropriately defended, but also to boost productivity and increase our economic growth into the future.

Andrew Messenger

Deaths in Queensland child protection system reach five-year high

Queensland has recorded a five-year high of 92 deaths in the child protection system, according to new data.

The Queensland Family and Child Commission reported the deaths of 452 children in its annual report, on Friday.

The figure included 102 Indigenous children. The report found 94 children died from “external causes”, including 28 from suicide and 13 from an accident or neglect. Meanwhile, 92 children had engaged with the state’s child safety system in the year before they died, while seven died in care and a further 43 had open investigations or “intake events”.

It is the highest number of deaths recorded in the state overall and the highest number in the child safety system in five years, up from 427 overall deaths and 57 in protection last year.

The commission, which also administrates the state’s child death review board, was created to independently oversee the child safety system as a result of a inquiry called by the state’s former premier Campbell Newman.

The state government recently tabled legislation to give the minister the power to sack its commissioner for any or no reason, but maintained the role would remain independent.

Tom McIlroy

‘Not entirely sure who they’re going to put in cuffs’, Hume says

Asked if possible legal action should be off the table, Hume said the liability was unclear:

“I’m not entirely sure who they’re going to put in cuffs,” she said.

The real alarm bell that was set off this week is the fact that the only reason we knew about this breach of the Medicare archive or data system is because OpenAI told us there was a breach.

If they hadn’t told us that there was a breach, would we have known about it at all? That demonstrates that our cyber defences, particularly for Services Australia, were woefully inadequate.

‘Finger-wagging’ over OpenAI hack not helpful: Jane Hume

Tom McIlroy

The deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, has expressed scepticism revelations an OpenAI agent accessed Australian government data without authorisation should have legal consequences for the company.

The hack was revealed last week, despite taking place in June. Government ministers have raised the prospect of possible referrals to the Australian federal police, but gaps in Australian law could make establishing criminal liability difficult.

Hume told ABC TV on Sunday that AI was inevitably going to be a part of Australia’s future and it was important the country was part of the conversation.

But certainly the way to go about that is not to threaten criminal action against US counterparts and those trusted partners that we’re relying on now to make sure that we can bring those frontier models, that we can do frontier model training here in Australia.

I don’t necessarily think that finger-wagging at our trusted partners, or trying to gazump Donald Trump, is the way to go about that.

Partner of NSW police officer who died says he’s lost the love of his life

Daniel Vasquez, the partner of NSW police officer Mia Lay, who died in a car crash while on duty, issued a statement on behalf of her family yesterday, saying he had lost the “love of my life”.

Vasquez said:

Mia loved what she did in the police. She was happy in the police, she was good at her job, and how loved she was by everyone in the community. She was the happiest girl I’ve met …

I’d ask for everyone to remember how stunning and beautiful she was. She was a kind hearted person, gave so much love to everyone that she cared about …

I’ve just lost the love of my life. She will be missed by everyone. And I ask that she is remembered.

Tom McIlroy

Marles defends Albanese’s global leadership award

Richard Marles has defended the prime minister Anthony Albanese’s decision to accept an award for global leadership in UN last week, part of a black tie event in Manhattan hosted by the Atlantic Council.

The opposition criticised Albanese for being in New York during difficult economic times for Australian households.

The prime minister accepted an award about the way in which we are managing our place in the world, and specifically our place in the region. In terms of the alliances that we’ve struck with countries around Australia, such as Papua New Guinea and Fiji, the way in which we are pursuing the AUKUS arrangements, which are building Australian capability in what is a very challenging world.

I think the recognition of the prime minister is deserved in respect of him. But it’s also a recognition of what his government has been doing to make sure that we are keeping Australians safe in a very challenging global environment, and that’s what we are seeking to do here.

Tom McIlroy

Trump White House wants Iran war to end: Marles

The defence minister, Richard Marles, is on News 24 this morning and has been asked about the ongoing economic and geopolitical damage being caused by Donald Trump’s war in Iran.

Marles says it clear that the White House wants the war to end.

Clearly, the United States wants to see an end to the conflict. That’s to state the obvious, but they are seeking to to manage that through

What is clear is that the global fuel supply chain is disrupted, and that is having an impact on the global economy ... and that’s what we are seeking to manage in terms of the way we manage the economy and the budget at home.

Marles says OpenAI CEO didn't tell him about hack in September meeting

Tom McIlroy

Richard Marles says revelations last week that an OpenAI agent hacked into Australian government websites is very serious, despite the nature of the information accessed being less sensitive.

Marles met with OpenAI boss Sam Altman earlier this month but the company did not disclose that it knew the agent had breached Australian government systems.

He declined to speculate about whether Altman knew about the breach or not when they met.

“The fact that we’ve got an artificial intelligence agent gaining unauthorised access to an Australian government website, that of itself is very serious,” Marles told News 24. “There’s no hiding that.

This is the first time this has happened in the context of Australia, and so we’re not shying away from that. In fact, the information that it obtained, was minor in its nature, in as much as that information we’ve now made public anyway, it wasn’t anyone’s personal data.

But in a sense, the seriousness doesn’t lie in the information that was obtained. It was the fact that we’ve got an unintended action of an AI agent gaining unauthorised access into an Australian government website.

Flight cancellations cause heartache for interstate footy fans

Caitlin Cassidy

Interstate footy fans grappled with flight delays and cancellations on Saturday as they raced to reach Melbourne in time for the AFL Grand Final.

Melbourne airport said some flights had been cancelled due to poor weather causing low visibility, with rain forecast for much of the morning and early afternoon.

About 100,000 fans packed into the MCG on Saturday for an all-interstate final between the Fremantle Dockers and the Brisbane Lions starting at 2.30pm.

A Qantas flight from Perth scheduled to land at 10.30am was cancelled and a further two were delayed, including another Qantas flight scheduled to arrive before the bounce at 1.40pm which was delayed by around an hour.

Two Brisbane flights were cancelled and nine were delayed by up to two hours, meaning some fans landed after the 2.30pm starting time.

Among those racing to make the game was journalist and TV host Brooke Boney, who was scheduled to land at 11.35am, which was pushed back by an hour. She made it to the ground just in time for Kylie Minogue’s pre-match entertainment.

Albanese says announcement of Medicare breach ‘purely in national interest’

Anthony Albanese says he was not aware of other cases of AI agents wrongfully accessing classified information before he revealed OpenAI’s unauthorised infiltration of the Medicare Statistics Reporting portal in New York on Thursday, Australian Associated Press reports.

“At the time we made our announcement … we weren’t aware of other occurrences,” the prime minister told reporters at Sydney airport on Saturday.

“We were acting purely in our national interest.”

The PM landed back in Australia on Saturday after a week in the US where he addressed the United Nations General Assembly on the international need to rein in AI.

He said news that autonomous agents allegedly infiltrated American university and commerce department sites, as well as the US Securities and Exchange Commission, further proved that need.

“We now know it wasn’t just the issue of the Australian sites that have been subject to AI agents accessing information without authorisation,” Albanese said.

What this does is confirm that approach of making sure that it needs to be an appropriate national response, as well as an international response to make sure that humans are in charge of this new and emerging technology.

Albanese said it was up to OpenAI to state why multiple breaches occurred.

Good morning

Welcome to our Sunday live blog. Flight delays and cancellations caused frustration and heartache for some footy fans racing to make it to Saturday’s AFL grand final before the first bounce. And the PM says the timing of his announcement of OpenAI’s Medicare hack was made “purely in the national interest”. More on both those stories shortly.

Also, the Liberal deputy leader, Jane Hume, will be speaking on the ABC’s Insiders this morning. More on that coming up.

australia.title: ‘Cash grab’: One Nation demands up to $630,000 from Victorian election candidates
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Many applicants left feeling ‘used, lied to, misled and gaslit’, complaint letter seen by Guardian Australia says Listen to th...
australia.content:
One Nation could collect as much as $633,000 from people who have put their hand up to run in the Victorian state election, with potential candidates questioning whether the party is staging a “cash grab”.

Guardian Australia has spoken to multiple former councillors, mayors and deputy mayors who expressed an interest in running for the party. They claim they went through what one called a “pay-to-play” application process, after which they were rejected.

Those who applied to be considered were required to pay $150 as a “non refundable application fee”, invoices seen by the Guardian show.

One Nation told the Guardian that 1,209 people put in an expression of interest to run in the November state election, and approximately 220 proceeded to the final stage, resulting in an estimated $33,000 flowing into party coffers if all final stage candidates paid this amount.

Applicants were also expected to be party members, with this translating to an additional $72,000 based on the minimum membership fee of $60 a year.

In addition, candidates were advised in interviews that they would be required to pay $5,500 of their own money to run if preselected, even though the vast majority of lower house electorates are not deemed winnable.

While it is not uncommon for the major parties to require candidates to pay an application fee, they do not levy campaign fees on candidates like those being charged by One Nation.

The candidate fee will bring $528,000 into the party’s coffers, based on running 88 lower house candidates and eight for the upper house. In total, the amount paid by candidates could be as much as $633,000.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Aidan McLindon, a political consultant who worked with One Nation in Victoria last year, said many potential candidates had been left frustrated by what appeared to be a “money-spinning exercise”.

One Nation was “disproportionately focusing on profits over policy”. McLindon said in an interview for episode three of The Populist, out on Monday.

Based on the party’s polling numbers, One Nation is also in line to receive as much as $10m through Victoria’s public electoral funding scheme.

Applicants who spoke to the Guardian have questioned whether the application process was genuine, saying the party had conducted 15-minute video interviews with each candidate before a decision was made. Potential candidates were all required to sign non-disclosure agreements about the process on application.

There is also concern that the upper house candidates were “captain’s picks” selected by the party’s state leader, Warren Pickering, with One Nation overlooking candidates with significant local government and professional experience.

A complaint letter sent to the party by one former Victorian mayor says the process has left many candidates feeling “that we were used, lied to, misled and gaslit”.

“The issue is that the process increasingly looks as though it was used as cover to conceal decisions that had already been substantially made, while creating the public appearance of an open, merit-based candidate search,” the letter seen by the Guardian states.

“Applicants should not have been encouraged to invest their time, energy, reputations and personal information in an elaborate exercise merely to provide legitimacy, numbers or political cover for what now appears to have been a biased and self-serving leadership process.”

Another local government member who had applied questioned whether the process was a “cash grab”.

“They are asking everyday folk, hard-working mums and dads, for $5,500 which is a lot of money,” one said.

“I just think it is a cash grab for the federal election. My feeling is they are just using all of the states to fundraise for the federal election where they want to take power.”

Another said they believed that under the party’s constitution, all funds would be transferred to One Nation’s Brisbane headquarters.

“They will get $800,000 in the kitty for doing absolutely nothing,” one said.

A spokesperson for One Nation said the party uses “a nominal cost recovery model to do police and other checks on candidate nominees”.

“All candidate fees have been paid into the Victorian state campaign account in accordance with the Victorian Electoral Commission rules.

“Application fees and campaign contributions are a standard requirement implemented by all major parties within Australia.”

The Guardian has previously reported that candidates at the 2025 federal election were left out of pocket by the party’s candidate funding agreements.

australia.title: Australian backlash to datacentres is faux import from US, officials say: ‘We are not the United States’
australia.snippet: Pro-datacentre officials argue scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and less damaging than in US Australian politicia...
australia.content:
Australian politicians and business leaders are arguing that their populace’s growing resentment of AI datacentres is an inauthentic import from the United States.

Like the US, Australia is seeing community resentment grow in response to a surge in the construction of massive AI datacentres. However, pro-datacentre officials and executives argue the scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and therefore less damaging than that in the US. They say the burgeoning negative reaction is being tainted and inflamed by a heated US debate that has arrived down under via social media feeds.

When the backlash began in earnest in the United States last year, it echoed slowly in Australia. In 2026, though, it has exploded into national conversation across the country, leading to calls for a national moratorium, community protests, three government inquiries, state frameworks being developed and the Australian government moving to set the rules for how the datacentres can be built, and how they consume energy and water.

Australian state governments, desperate for economic growth, have been broadly welcoming of the investment for the new centres, in some cases overriding local council approval processes, given the size of the projects being developed.

In July, Victoria’s then-minister for economic growth, Steve Dimopoulos, boasted that his state was second only to New South Wales in terms of datacentres, and was outstripping Australia’s most populous state in growth for new centres. He expressed concern that the growing resentment toward new developments was a result of US social media influence.

“We’re seeing some US states move to ban new large datacentres. And those campaigns and mega-developments in the US shape public opinion in Australia,” he said. “Because when it’s on your phone, you think it’s right here, or you think it might just come here.”

The minister declared: “We are not the United States. Our planning, energy and water systems are much more carefully monitored, managed and regulated.”

Leaders in the datacentre sector have also complained about the backlash, calling it misleading and disingenuous.

“Australia’s datacentre debate is being fought on America’s facts,” Belinda Dennett, the head of the peak lobby group for the sector, Data Centres Australia, declared in a speech in March.

Dennett said reactions to datacentres from everyday people range from curiosity to confusion and fear, and the news around the sector was “alarming”.

“The industry is depicted as energy vampires, water hogs and job killers,” she said. “The problem is that most of those headlines originate in the United States, where the industry is operating at a completely different scale, under completely different market rules. They are being transplanted wholesale into Australian debates as though the contexts were interchangeable.”

Dennett said the US has 5,400 datacentres, with 53.7 gigawatts of total capacity, compared with 252 in Australia with 1.4 gigawatts of capacity. Measurements of the number of US datacentres vary.

“When people read about datacentres straining the grid, driving up bills and consuming vast amounts of water, they are reading about America’s challenges, applied uncritically to an Australian market that bears almost no resemblance to it,” she said.

What Dennett omitted was that Australia, with a population of 28 million, has just under one datacentre per 100,000 people, compared with 1.5 per 100,000 people in the US, population 342.7 million.

The pace of datacentre construction is increasing rapidly in Australia, with several large datacentres with 1 gigawatts or more capacity in the planning.

Trending videos on TikTok and Instagram highlight major local community concerns including a 2.4 gigawatt centre planned for outer Melbourne, and a 2 gigawatt gas-powered centre in the Northern Territory.

That is the equivalent of 2m households’ annual electricity consumption, said Rob Nicholls, professor and senior research associate in digital policy at the University of Sydney. The NT’s population is just over 265,000.

The Australian government – seeing the US gas boom fueled by datacentres’ demand for power – has planned to override states and ban gas being used to power centres. New rules would require datacentres’ operators to bring as much new renewable energy into the system as the centre would otherwise take.

Some experts find the backlash justified in following the US example.

“The social media input from the US is very vocal and rationally based: ‘It’s going to increase the cost of electricity and it’s going to increase the cost of water and I don’t get a benefit from it.’ And that’s a rational position,” said Nicholls.

Nicholls said the hurdle facing the Australian government is explaining to its constituents how the issues faced in the United States differ from local ones.

Legislation for the framework is unlikely to arrive until next year, and has led to calls for Australia to follow the lead of New York and implement a moratorium on new development until proper rules are in place.

Until then, there are now two state inquiries and one federal inquiry into the sector, along with the steady stream of new development applications leading to pushback from locals.

Many of Australia’s datacentres are US-owned. The federal assistant minister for technology, Andrew Charlton, said that Australians may be cynical about datacentres in their communities because many of the companies that operate the facilities are not Australian. Microsoft and Amazon operate several, and OpenAI and Anthropic are eyeing their own developments.

“Simply building datacentres in Australia does not necessarily mean that Australia captures the economics of AI,” he said in a speech this week. “We can supply the land, we can supply the electricity, we can host the machines, and still find that much of the value – and many of the economic rents – flow offshore.”

Charlton called for datacentre providers who want to build in Australia to enable access to compute for Australian start-ups, researchers and not-for-profits, on favourable terms, and flagged that Australia could build its own local AI capability based on open-weight models.

“We risk becoming dependent on imported intelligence itself,” Charlton said.

australia.title: I was focused on becoming the first Aboriginal tennis champion. Then one remark changed something in me
australia.snippet: As a teenager in Sydney, the would-be Wimbledon champion was working towards a singular goal when an act of racism shattered her naivety ...
australia.content:
It was a regular match. Until it wasn’t. In 1969, I was 17 and had been living in Sydney with my tennis coach, Vic Edwards, and his family for several years. I had left my home town of Barellan – on Wirajudjuri country in the Riverina region of New South Wales – to pursue my tennis dreams in the big smoke.

The year before, I had finished high school at Willoughby girls high – where I was the only Aboriginal student – and I was doing my secretarial course in the city. The Metropolitan Business College where I studied was conveniently located near the headquarters of the Foundation for Aboriginal Affairs.

The idea for the foundation was to give city-based Aboriginal people a cultural hub where we could come together and find support. I was spending more and more time there with my friends Isabel and Bob, the latter whom I was casually dating.

Isabel and Bob were young and lots of fun but they were also acutely aware of the politics of being Black. I was naive to the injustices of Australia – and the world – and I learned a lot from Isabel and the guys at the foundation.

At the time, I was focused on a single goal: to become the first Aboriginal tennis champion. To achieve that goal, I had to shut myself off from everything other than tennis. That included politics.

I was training for my upcoming European tour, and part of program included playing doubles with Vic Edwards’ daughter, Trisha, at the White City badge competition twice a week. Trisha and I had been playing together for years and were quite the pair. We were the “tennis twins”, in our matching dresses, at tournaments.

It was during our usual doubles game at White City against two older women that something happened. Trisha and I convincingly won against our opponents, and we went to the net to shake their hands. As we reached over the net, though, one of the ladies turned to her partner and said, “That’s the first time I’ve ever been beaten by a n*****r.”

The N-word. I had never been called it before. I went into shock.

The word took a moment to sink in. At first, I thought I had misheard. But then Trisha responded with a cutting comment and I knew it was real. Still, the moment felt far away, as though it was happening to someone else.

The older women left and I remained at the net with Trisha. Suddenly, we were crying. We both stood in the centre of the court, hugging and sobbing. The word had wounded me like a paper cut, innocuous at first, then stinging. I’m not sure why that single word had such a dramatic effect on me. It wasn’t even an Australian slander. The N-word was a cheap, American slur that reminded me of fake soap-opera trash talk. But when it was directed at me, it felt very real. Was this the way it was going to be out there in the mean streets of tennis?

Still sobbing, I called the first person I thought of: Isabel at the foundation. Through tears, I told her what happened. “You jump in a taxi and get here right now,” she said.

When I arrived, I was greeted by Isabel and Bob. They held me and patted my back as I cried in their arms. Isabel said she had never seen me so upset. We sat around and drank cups of coffee for hours, talking it over. “It’s OK,” Bob told me, kindly. “These things happen to us all the time. You just have to deal with it, and you can. You’re strong.”

Something had irrevocably changed within me. My naivety had been broken. The protective bubble my family and the Edwardses had built around me had been smashed. I would move on but I would never be the same innocent young girl.

When I got back to the house hours later, Trisha had already relayed the events to Mr Edwards. I was glad to have missed his initial fury at the incident. Mr Edwards – who was quick to anger – was remarkably matter-of-fact. He had informed the NSW Lawn Tennis Association over the phone and was in the middle of writing an official complaint. “We have to deal with this in the proper manner, through the correct channels,” he said.

I don’t know what happened as a result of the call or the complaint. But I never saw the woman at White City again.

After that, I spent more and more time at the foundation. My friends there reminded me of my people but not in a way that made me homesick; instead, they gave me a sense of feeling good about being Aboriginal. Proud – that was it! They made me feel proud to be Aboriginal.

When I went on to win my first Wimbledon singles tournament two years later in 1971 – becoming the first Aboriginal woman to claim the title – the win was for all Aboriginal people.

I like to think I was doing my part in my own way – by breaking new ground, taking up space and inspiring the next generation of hopeful Aboriginal athletes.

I hope I have paved the way for our young ones, and that the road is a lot smoother these days.

world.title: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys
world.snippet: Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer Cape Town’s c...
world.content:
Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming into repeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered.

Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A 2025 census found that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops.

As a result of the population boom, troops of chacma baboons on the city’s peninsula regularly rip off roof sheeting, sneak into unlocked cars and raid food pantries. Some monkeys are now staying up late into the night to break into homes in Simon’s Town and nab snacks from convenience stores. Residents can no longer barbecue or host garden parties for fear of the marauding baboons.

“It’s depreciated property values because it’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces and paw prints, and you know they’re coming every day,” said Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town who has long studied the local baboons.

Cape Town’s geography is partially to blame. Much of the problem is confined to the Cape Peninsula, a narrow sliver of land stretching from the city centre to Cape Point. Here, baboons are boxed in between the steep, protected area of Table Mountain national park and the sprawling urban development that stretches to the Atlantic Ocean.

“The underlying issue is that baboons will seek low-lying land. That is their natural drive – it’s better access to water and more productive vegetation,” said Joselyn Mormile, who leads the Cape Baboon Partnership (CBP), a nonprofit organisation that works with the city and local conservation authorities to manage the baboons. “But throughout the peninsula, we’ve developed most of those places. It’s a constant battle between the two.”

Initially, the CBP’s 2025 management plan proposed to move four troops to a sanctuary. That was revised, Mormile said, to give two other troops living in the northern section of the peninsula “the benefit of the doubt to see if they can adjust in that remaining space … We believe that they could settle quite nicely.”

The baboons have proved an especially divisive – and expensive – issue. Cape Town’s baboon management programme costs about 20m rand for 18 months (£920,000), with full-time rangers watching over most of the troops to try to head off any trouble.

In addition to moving the Waterfall and Seaforth troops to a sanctuary, a baboon-proof northern boundary fence will be erected between urban areas and nearby mountains.

Animal rights activists, who have been staging peaceful protests for months, and some scientists say the city should build a fence to exclude the Waterfall and Seaforth troops rather than remove the animals from their environment.

However, O’Riain said it was likely that the baboons would simply move along to the next area of low-lying land where the fence ends, as there was not enough food for the baboons behind the proposed southern fenced area.

Opponents argue that removing the other baboons will cause long-term psychological distress and social disruption, and that the baboons play an important ecological role by dispersing plant seeds.

Chacma baboons are not considered endangered. And the welfare of the animals is already in question: baboons are being poisoned, hit by cars, chased by dogs and shot.

“No one should ever shoot a baboon, but if people feel the authorities are not doing anything, they will take action – and that action is never nice,” O’Riain said. “Just a few days ago, a baboon was shot straight through the chest.

“How many more millions of rand are we going to throw into these troops only to end up in exactly the same place in another 10 years’ time?” he said. “Which is shocking baboon welfare, shocking baboon health, and a very poor quality of life for the people who are living in these areas.”

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

world.title: At least 27 dead after two mass shootings in South Africa, police say
world.snippet: Seventeen people killed at bar near Johannesburg and 10 killed in separate incident at barbecue venue near Cape Town Two separate mass sh...
world.content:
Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, police have said.

The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 assault rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, south-west of Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said.

In a separate statement, police said 10 people had been killed in a mass shooting at an entertainment venue selling grilled meat, known as a shisanyama, in Lwandle, near Cape Town. Another 11 people were wounded in that shooting. Police said they were searching for multiple suspects, without giving an exact number.

The two attacks happened days after a mass shooting by three gunmen at a house party near the east coast city of Durban killed 11 people, including a pregnant woman.

No arrests had been made in the two latest mass shootings, police said.

South Africa has struggled with high rates of violent crime for years, but the series of mass shootings this week were shocking even to a country used to some of the highest violent crime rates in the world.

Police in the province of Gauteng said on Sunday morning they had launched a manhunt for the unidentified eight suspects in the Johannesburg tavern shooting, with no arrests yet made.

“It is alleged that patrons were drinking inside and outside the tavern when the suspects arrived and opened fire on those outside,” a police spokesperson, Capt Tintswalo Sibeko, said in a statement.

“The suspects then entered the tavern and continued shooting at patrons inside. The suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols. They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident.”

Western Cape police said they had set up a team led by serious violent crime detectives to investigate the Cape Town shooting, in which the gunmen entered the shinsanyama venue at about 1.46am on Saturday night and starting shooting at customers.

“Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities,” the statement said. “Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained … Detectives are hard at work in search of the perpetrators of the shooting incident with no arrests effected yet. The identities of the deceased persons will be released once their next of kin are informed.”

In the 12 months to 30 June, more than 22,700 people were murdered in South Africa, according to police data.

South Africans are already reeling after the discovery of numerous women’s bodies near Johannesburg’s airport since July, most of which were found in the last few weeks. The killings led to renewed anger about high rates of gender-based violence in the country and has piled pressure on police and politicians to do more about it.

Associated Press in Cape Town contributed to this report

world.title: Rebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil war
world.snippet: Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government There are growing fears of a retu...
world.content:
There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.

About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 during a devastating war between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.

On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including the TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”.

The TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border.

Flights to the historic Ethiopian town of Lalibela were also suspended on Thursday because of nearby fighting, while people in Tigray stocked up ⁠on food and cash, with one resident telling Reuters that people there feared they could face siege conditions similar to those during the previous war.

A resident of Adigrat, a city close to the Eritrean border, ‌described panic-buying and shops emptying. “Food shortages are worsening as market shelves sit empty … Essential medicines remain scarce and astronomically expensive,” he told Reuters. “Daily survival has become a constant calculation.”

The TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.

The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital.

In its first public comments on the fighting, Ethiopia’s army said on ⁠Thursday it had foiled the attacks and killed, wounded or captured more than 500 enemy fighters.

Analysts say the TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s​ neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.”

The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, when Eritrea and Fano, an insurgent group that is now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans.

Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours.

Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while ​with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea ​has repeatedly denied similar accusations.

The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war.

The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge ​yet to the 2022 Pretoria agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed.

It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea.

On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, urged “utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks. An EU spokesperson called for “immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria agreement.

In the 2020-22 war, Tigray was largely cut off from the outside world as communications were severed, and access to food, cash and medicines was severely restricted, pushing hundreds of thousands of people into famine-like conditions.

AFP and Reuters contributed reporting

world.title: Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in years
world.snippet: Sunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock market Nils Pratley: Does this mark the end of London’s ...
world.content:
A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.

Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.

The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.

Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.

Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.

“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.

“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”

Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”

Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.

Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.

Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, ​Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.

Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.

The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.

Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

world.title: Top South African police officer charged with raping woman, 18, and grooming 16-year-old girl
world.snippet: Arrest of Shadrack Sibiya comes as country reels from cases of femicide and alleged police corruption and criminality One of South Africa...
world.content:
One of South Africa’s most senior police officers has been charged with raping an 18-year-old woman and grooming a 16-year-old girl, as the country’s police face allegations of corruption and failing to tackle violence against women and girls.

Shadrack Sibiya, who was already suspended from his role as deputy national police commissioner over allegations he interfered with political killings investigations, was arrested on Monday. He is facing charges of rape, people trafficking, promoting the sexual grooming of a child and two counts of grooming a child.

Sibiya appeared briefly in a Johannesburg court on Tuesday. He was then taken to prison in the capital, Pretoria, before a bail hearing on 29 September, as prosecutors had argued he was an escape risk.

South Africa is reeling after the discovery of nine women’s bodies across Ekurhuleni, the municipality east of Johannesburg, in September. Meanwhile, the Madlanga Commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police for the last year.

Puleng Dimpane, the acting national police commissioner, said: “Police officers are entrusted with protecting women and children. They cannot themselves be implicated in conduct that undermines this responsibility. As the country continues to confront the scourge of gender-based violence and femicide, there can be no room for anyone within the police service who is alleged to abuse their position or violate the rights of women and children.”

Sibiya is accused of raping an 18-year-old woman at a hotel in May in the Sandton business district of Johannesburg. The alleged rape took place “whilst she was passed out due to intoxication administered by the accused”, according to a copy of the charge sheet.

The alleged grooming of the 16-year-old girl took place over WhatsApp between 20 July and 3 August, according to the charge sheet. This allegedly included Sibiya sending the girl naked photos of herself, which she had not sent to him.

Sibiya did not enter a plea at the hearing on Tuesday. His lawyer told the court that they needed more time to consult with and get instructions from him, according to News24.

Firoz Cachalia, the acting police minister, said: “We strongly condemn the alleged conduct.

“Where allegations of sexual offences are made against a member of the service, they must be investigated without fear or favour.”

When Sibiya appeared before the Madlanga Commission in February he denied allegations that he had moved 121 political killings investigations from KwaZulu-Natal province to the national head office without explanation.

Sibiya also denied that he had received a gift of 20 impalas from Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, a businessman who received an allegedly fraudulent 360m rand (£16.7m) police health services contract soon after the alleged gift.

Matlala, who has been charged with attempted murder, alongside several other charges including fraud and money laundering, declined to comment on the impalas when he appeared at the Madlanga Commission in August. He said he did not want to incriminate himself as the matter was under investigation.
